title: Social justice gains coexist with persistent informality, unequal power, weak bargaining rights, and transition risks
source_unit: International Labour Organization, The State of Social Justice 2025: A Work in Progress
geography: Global comparison of social-justice indicators, with qualitative findings from 17 countries

observations.period: 1995-2024; poverty, child labour, and social capability

denominator.unit: global population and worker/child-labour indicators summarized by the ILO

child_labour_1995.unit: percent of children in child labour in 1995

child_labour_2024.unit: percent of children in child labour in 2024

extreme_poverty.value: fell from roughly four in ten people in 1995 to roughly one in ten in 2023

working_poverty_2024.unit: percent of workers in working poverty in 2024

observations.method: ILO synthesis of global labour, poverty, education, rights, and capability indicators across multiple data systems and reference years.
observations.uncertainty: Indicators use different definitions, sources, and reference periods; global progress does not show distribution within countries or prove that social-justice institutions caused the changes.
observations.subgroup: Children, workers, people in poverty, countries and regions with different income and labour-market structures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate progress can coexist with insecurity, exclusion, and reversible gains; falling prevalence does not mean harms have disappeared or that affected groups experience equal access to rights.

denominator.unit: global working population and income/wealth distribution indicators

people_below_three_dollars.unit: millions of people living on less than 3 US dollars per day

top_one_percent_income.unit: percent of global income held by the top 1 percent

top_one_percent_wealth.unit: percent of global wealth held by the top 1 percent

informal_employment.unit: percent of workers in informal employment

collective_bargaining.value: compliance scores for freedom of association and collective bargaining rights are deteriorating

observations.method: ILO compilation of income, wealth, poverty, employment-status, and labour-rights indicators with analysis of distribution and institutions.
observations.uncertainty: Income and wealth shares, informality, and rights scores have different measurement frameworks and country coverage; they do not identify individual earnings, bargaining episodes, or enforcement outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Informal workers, low-income workers, workers lacking collective voice, and populations affected by wealth and income concentration.
observations.counterinterpretation: Informal work can provide entry and income where formal jobs are scarce, while formal status alone does not guarantee decent work, voice, or security.

denominator.unit: countries contributing qualitative interviews and lived-justice evidence to the report

institutional_trust.value: interview evidence points to a widespread crisis of institutional trust

formal_lived_gap.value: workers report exclusion, mistreatment, and neglect despite strong legal frameworks

justice_as_institutional_choice.value: economic growth does not automatically produce justice; political will, institutional reform, and inclusive governance shape outcomes

observations.method: ILO report synthesis of interviews from 17 countries alongside global social-justice indicators and labour-rights analysis.
observations.uncertainty: Interview findings are qualitative and purposive rather than representative of all workers; reported experiences should not be generalized into respondent-level prevalence or causal estimates.
observations.subgroup: Workers and institutions in 17 countries, with attention to exclusion, mistreatment, neglect, legal protections, and trust.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal rights can provide an important platform for remedy even when implementation is incomplete; perceived injustice can vary with expectations, sector, identity, and local institutions.

observations.period: 2025 onward; climate, technology, and demographic transitions

denominator.unit: major societal transitions identified by the ILO report

transitions.value: climate, technological, and demographic transitions are expected to reshape work and justice

institutional_response.value: labour institutions should be applied, adapted, and amplified across transition policy silos

fair_distribution.value: fair transition requires attention to how opportunities and risks are distributed across groups

observations.method: ILO synthesis of labour institutions, social-justice indicators, and transition policy analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The framework identifies policy directions rather than estimating the effects of a specific reform; transition impacts vary by sector, geography, gender, age, skill, and institutional capacity.
observations.subgroup: Workers, employers, governments, social partners, communities, and people exposed to climate, technology, and demographic change.
observations.counterinterpretation: Existing institutions may be too rigid or unevenly accessible to manage new transitions; adaptation can expand inclusion but can also dilute protections if bargaining power is weak.

related_sources.claim: ILO Employment and Social Trends 2026 provides complementary current labour-market and job-quality estimates.
ILO World Social Protection Report 2024-26 provides complementary coverage and just-transition evidence.

boundary: This record adds a social-justice route linking poverty, informality, distribution, labour rights, institutional trust, and climate, technological, and demographic transitions. It uses aggregate indicators and a report-level qualitative synthesis, not respondent-level interview analysis, individual worker histories, causal institutional estimates, or claims that legal protection guarantees lived justice.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ILO State of Social Justice 2025 page and report summary were reviewed for poverty, child labour, informality, distribution, bargaining rights, interview scope, institutional trust, and fair-transition claims.
